1.1

Preliminaries and Definitions for the Point Star Unfolding

Definition 1 Let P be a convex polyhedron, and let x be a point on P. The star unfolding, Sₓ, is a 2-dimensional polygon formed by cutting P along a shortest path from every vertex of P to x, and flattening the result into the plane. See Fig. 2. Note that there is a choice of cuts if a vertex has more than one shortest path to x.

ConvexPolyhedron is the convex hull of its exact extreme vertices in ℝ³, with nonempty interior. The current starCuts removes straight source-to-vertex segments. These are shortest surface cuts when the source is cofacial with every vertex. This is not yet a definition of an arbitrary choice of shortest cuts for an arbitrary source.

If P has n vertices, then the polygon Sₓ will have 2n vertices in general, and 2(n − 1) vertices if x is located at a vertex of P. The vertices of Sₓ alternate around the boundary between vertex images, denoted vᵢ, that correspond to the vertices of P, and n ‘copies’ of x, called source images and denoted by xᵢ. See Fig. 2. The edges of Sₓ correspond to the shortest path cuts made from each vertex to x. Therefore, the two edges incident to any vertex image vᵢ are always the same length.

The cut locus (or “ridge tree”), Tₓ, is the closure of the set of all points on the surface of P that have more than one shortest path to x. It is known that the cut locus is a tree [12], and that its edges are shortest paths [1] and thus correspond to straight-line segments in Sₓ. See Fig. 2b. As a corollary to their proof of non-overlap [3, Thm. 10.2], Aronov and O’Rourke proved that the cut locus is a subset of the Voronoi diagram of the images of x, but we will not use this result.

1.2

Preliminaries and Definitions for the Geodesic Star Unfolding

Lean annotation: included for completeness; curve-source unfolding is outside this point-star formalization. Continue to the point proof →

Given a polyhedron P, a geodesic curve λ on P is a curve on the surface of P, such that at every interior point p of λ, the surface angle to either side of p is exactly π. If the surface angle to either side of p is at most π then the curve is called a quasigeodesic. We will only consider [quasi]geodesic curves that are simple, meaning there is no point of self-intersection between any two interior (i.e., non-endpoint) points of the curve.

The endpoints of λ are labelled a and b and the two sides of λ are labelled s and t, with the convention that the clockwise order around λ on the outside surface of P is a, s, b, t. We distinguish shortest paths to λ that arrive at (or “report to”) a or b, and shortest paths that arrive at interior points of λ on side s or t. Any shortest path that arrives at an interior point of λ forms a right angle with λ, as shown by the following lemma, which is a special case of [9, Lem. 1].

In the unfolding Sλ, a source image is either a copy of an endpoint (a or b), called a point image, or a sub-segment of λ corresponding to side s or t, called a segment image. (Note that a segment image might include one of the endpoints of λ.) Around a clockwise traversal of the boundary of Sλ we encounter source images in order a, s, b, t—this is because our convention is to draw the inside of the polyhedron’s surface facing up. Each consecutive pair of source images is separated by two edges of equal length joined at a vertex image, such that the edges correspond to the shortest path cut at the vertex.

The cut locus of a geodesic λ, denoted Tλ, is the closure of the set of all points on the surface of P that have more than one shortest path to λ. The cut locus of a geodesic is a tree [13]. (An alternate proof can be found in [4, Lem. 4]. The lemma applies to the outside of any closed convex curve on the surface of P—in the present situation, the closed convex curve is the set of points at some fixed distance ε from λ.) See ahead to Fig. 6.

A key difference from the point case is that the edges of the geodesic cut locus are not necessarily straight-line segments. Every edge of the cut locus is the locus of points that are equidistant from two source images. Thus, when the two sources to either side of an edge are a point image and a segment image respectively, a parabolic cut locus edge will result. The cut locus edges between pairs of point images or pairs of segment images will still be straight.

2

New Proof for the Point Star Unfolding

In this section we give a new proof of non-overlap for the point star unfolding that is simpler than the original proof of Aronov and O’Rourke [3].

The most important idea of our proof is to partition the star unfolding into pairs of congruent triangles. Each vertex of the cut locus has three or more shortest paths to x on the surface of P. Add all these shortest paths as line segments in the star unfolding. We use the following basic properties of shortest paths: (1) no two shortest paths to x (or more generally, to a geodesic curve) cross each other [9, Lem. 2] (their lemma is stated for vertices of the polyhedron, but applies more generally); and (2) no shortest path crosses the cut locus [12, Lem. 4.2]. These properties imply that when we add the line segments corresponding to shortest paths between x and cut locus vertices, each edge of the cut locus will have a triangle to each side. Because all shortest paths from a cut locus vertex to the nearest source images have the same length, the two triangles to either side of a cut locus edge have corresponding sides of equal length, and therefore are congruent. We call each such pair of triangles a kite. The kite associated with cut locus edge e is denoted kite(e). The two images of x to each side of e are called the apex vertices of the kite. Observe that the kites form a partition of Sₓ. See Fig. 2b.

We define the source angle of e, α(e), to be the interior angle at either apex of kite(e). See Fig. 2b. We extend this definition to paths as follows. For a path σ of cut locus edges, where σ = e₁, …, eₜ, the source angle of σ is α(σ) = ∑i=1tα(ei). Observe that α(σ) ≤ π because 2α(σ) measures the total source angle at both apex vertices of every kite on the path, so this is bounded by the total surface angle at the source point x, which is bounded by 2π.

cofacial_star_embedding constructs a continuous open embedding of the actual retained surface into the plane, with bounded connected image, finite straight-segment boundary, and exact local intrinsic isometry. This is a real proved checkpoint, but it is not Theorem 1 for every convex polyhedron and source. The cofacial hypothesis is impossible for the all-triangular octahedron, so this does not claim all four graph models admit such a source.

  1. Construct the cut tree and coherent, covering radial charts.
  2. Prove the angle budget and separate every pair of kites.
  3. Glue the triangle maps and construct inverse neighborhoods.

  5. Identify the exact finite-segment boundary.

Proof We will show that no two kites overlap. Consider two kites, and the path in the cut locus between them. Let e₁,..., eₜ be the edges of the path in the cut locus with eᵢ joining cut locus vertices pᵢ₋₁ and pᵢ. Let kᵢ = kite(eᵢ ). We will show that k₁ and kₜ have disjoint interiors. We will define a sequence of regions W₁,..., Wₜ₋₁, called W-wedges, so that Wᵢ includes k₁,..., kᵢ and excludes kᵢ₊₁. Then Wₜ₋₁ includes k₁ and excludes kₜ, which will complete the proof.

The boundary of the W-wedge Wᵢ consists of four edges, generally shaped like a ‘W’ and defined as follows. The center point of Wᵢ is the point pᵢ, where eᵢ and eᵢ₊₁ intersect; the inner legs are the edges of kᵢ that are incident to pᵢ; and the outer legs form an angle with the inner legs (on the side of kᵢ) of π/2 + αᵢ, where αᵢ = ∑j=1iα(ej). The outer legs extend either to their point of intersection, or as infinite rays if they do not intersect. This boundary divides the plane into two regions and we define Wᵢ to be the region containing kᵢ in a neighbourhood of pᵢ. We also define W₀ to have center point p₀, with inner legs along the edges of k₁ and outer legs rotated outward (on the opposite side from k₁) by π/2. See Fig. 4. Note that αᵢ is in the range [0, π] as observed above.

Scope of this correspondence: Sets in the plane and affine isometric changes of coordinates.

Explanation, scope and remaining work

The Lean induction tracks three facts separately: the old wedge is contained in an enlarged wedge, the enlarged wedge avoids the next kite’s interior, and moving coordinates turns their union into the new wedge. It explicitly transports every kite into one common plane.

How the proof is split

  1. contains: Wᵢ₋₁ ⊆ W′ᵢ.
  2. avoids: W′ᵢ ∩ interior(kᵢ) = ∅.
  3. updated: Wᵢ is the transported union W′ᵢ ∪ kᵢ.
  4. Finite induction carries all earlier regions forward and separates the endpoints.

Explanation, scope and remaining work

The Lean induction tracks three facts separately: the old wedge is contained in an enlarged wedge, the enlarged wedge avoids the next kite’s interior, and moving coordinates turns their union into the new wedge. It explicitly transports every kite into one common plane.

How the proof is split

  2. avoids: W′ᵢ ∩ interior(kᵢ) = ∅.
  3. updated: Wᵢ is the transported union W′ᵢ ∪ kᵢ.
  4. Finite induction carries all earlier regions forward and separates the endpoints.

Note that the unfolding does not overlap in the neighbourhood of point pᵢ—this is true whether pᵢ is a point with 2π surface area, or a vertex, which will be incident to a single cut. Thus the kites kᵢ and kᵢ₋₁, which are both incident to pᵢ, do not overlap. Rotate each of the inner legs of Wᵢ₋₁ about point pᵢ₋₁, away from kᵢ₋₁ to the edge of kᵢ. This is a rotation by 0° when an edge of kᵢ₋₁ is coincident with an edge of kᵢ. Keep the angle between inner and outer legs fixed throughout the rotation. Observe that all the kite edges incident to pᵢ₋₁ have the same length, so we really perform a rigid transformation on each half of the W. Call the resulting W-wedge W′ᵢ (shown as a dashed poly-line in Fig. 4). Notice that W′ᵢ contains Wᵢ₋₁, because the angle αᵢ₋₁ + π/2 is in the range [π/2, 3π/2] so the outer legs remain outside the rotation sector of the inner legs. (Here it is crucial that we added the extra π/2 to the initial angle.) That kᵢ is outside W′ᵢ follows from applying Lemma 2 to the outside of W′ᵢ, noting that αᵢ₋₁ + α(eᵢ) ≤ π so the angle αᵢ₋₁ + π/2 is in the range [π/2, 3π/2 − α(eᵢ)] and therefore the complementary angle is in the range [α(eᵢ) + π/2, 3π/2].

wedge_step_with_parametersTheorem · Proof checked

SixVertexUnfolding.ConvexPolyhedron.JunctionFan.wedge_step_with_parameters

Hypotheses and surrounding Lean context
open Real Set EuclideanGeometry Wedge
variable {P : ConvexPolyhedron} {a : frontier P.body} {T : P.CutLocusTree a}
  {u : T.vertices} (fan : JunctionFan T u)
theorem wedge_step_with_parameters
    (incoming outgoing : circularGapMidpoints fan.order.angles fan.order.first fan.order.last)
    (distinct : incoming ≠ outgoing) (ω : ℝ) (outer_lower : π / 2 ≤ ω)
    (budget : ω + (fan.triangles outgoing).model.sourceAngle ≤ 3 * π / 2) :
    let z := fan.order.chart.origin
    let d := P.surfaceDist a (T.vertexTarget u)
    let L := dist (u : Space) ((fan.order.neighbors outgoing).val : Space)
    let y := z + L • direction outgoing
    ∃ α β γ δ : ℝ,
      IsCircularGap fan.order.angles fan.order.first fan.order.last α β ∧
      IsCircularGap fan.order.angles fan.order.first fan.order.last γ δ ∧
      (incoming : ℝ) = (α + β) / 2 ∧ (outgoing : ℝ) = (γ + δ) / 2 ∧
      ∃ D Θ : ℝ, 0 < D ∧ 0 < Θ ∧ Θ < π ∧
        D = P.surfaceDist a (T.vertexTarget (fan.order.neighbors outgoing).val) ∧
        π - Θ = angle (fan.triangles outgoing).model.first
          (fan.triangles outgoing).model.right (fan.triangles outgoing).model.left ∧
        let W := {x | x - z ∈ polarRegion d ω α β}
        let V := {x | x - z ∈ polarRegion d ω δ (γ + 2 * π)}
        let W' := {x | x - y ∈ polarRegion D (ω + (fan.triangles outgoing).model.sourceAngle)
          (Θ + (γ + δ) / 2) (2 * π - Θ + (γ + δ) / 2)}
        W ⊆ V ∧ Disjoint V (interior (gapKite z d L γ δ)) ∧ W' = V ∪ gapKite z d L γ δ

SixVertexUnfolding.ConvexPolyhedron.JunctionFan.wedge_step_with_parameters

Hypotheses and surrounding Lean context
open Real Set EuclideanGeometry Wedge
variable {P : ConvexPolyhedron} {a : frontier P.body} {T : P.CutLocusTree a}
  {u : T.vertices} (fan : JunctionFan T u)
theorem wedge_step_with_parameters
    (incoming outgoing : circularGapMidpoints fan.order.angles fan.order.first fan.order.last)
    (distinct : incoming ≠ outgoing) (ω : ℝ) (outer_lower : π / 2 ≤ ω)
    (budget : ω + (fan.triangles outgoing).model.sourceAngle ≤ 3 * π / 2) :
    let z := fan.order.chart.origin
    let d := P.surfaceDist a (T.vertexTarget u)
    let L := dist (u : Space) ((fan.order.neighbors outgoing).val : Space)
    let y := z + L • direction outgoing
    ∃ α β γ δ : ℝ,
      IsCircularGap fan.order.angles fan.order.first fan.order.last α β ∧
      IsCircularGap fan.order.angles fan.order.first fan.order.last γ δ ∧
      (incoming : ℝ) = (α + β) / 2 ∧ (outgoing : ℝ) = (γ + δ) / 2 ∧
      ∃ D Θ : ℝ, 0 < D ∧ 0 < Θ ∧ Θ < π ∧
        D = P.surfaceDist a (T.vertexTarget (fan.order.neighbors outgoing).val) ∧
        π - Θ = angle (fan.triangles outgoing).model.first
          (fan.triangles outgoing).model.right (fan.triangles outgoing).model.left ∧
        let W := {x | x - z ∈ polarRegion d ω α β}
        let V := {x | x - z ∈ polarRegion d ω δ (γ + 2 * π)}
        let W' := {x | x - y ∈ polarRegion D (ω + (fan.triangles outgoing).model.sourceAngle)
          (Θ + (γ + δ) / 2) (2 * π - Θ + (γ + δ) / 2)}
        W ⊆ V ∧ Disjoint V (interior (gapKite z d L γ δ)) ∧ W' = V ∪ gapKite z d L γ δ

Our proof, like Aronov and O’Rourke’s, shows a stronger result that certain regions outside the star unfolding are empty. Aronov and O’Rourke [3] showed that at any vertex vᵢ adjacent to source images xᵢ and xᵢ₊₁ in the unfolding, no part of the unfolding enters the circular sector centered at vᵢ exterior to the unfolding near vᵢ and bounded by the radii vᵢ xᵢ and vᵢ xᵢ₊₁. See Fig. 5. Our proof shows that larger regions are empty, as formalized in the following lemma.

    (steps : ∀ i : Fin n, RegionStep (regions i) (regions (i + 1)) (kites i)) :

Lemma 3 Let vᵢ be a vertex image adjacent to source images xᵢ and xᵢ₊₁ on the boundary of a star unfolding Sₓ, and let W be the region bounded by vᵢ xᵢ, vᵢ xᵢ₊₁, and the rays extending from xᵢ and xᵢ₊₁ at right angles from these segments on the exterior side of vᵢ. Then no part of the unfolding intersects the interior of W.

Proof In non-degenerate situations, vᵢ is a leaf of the cut locus. Let e be the cut locus edge incident to vᵢ. For any kite k = kite( f ) of the unfolding, consider the path in the cut locus starting with e and ending with f, and apply the above proof to this path. Wedge W in the statement of the lemma is wedge W₀ in the proof, and the proof shows that kite k does not enter wedge W₀.

More generally, vᵢ may be an internal vertex of the cut locus with more than one incident cut locus edge, and we need a slight generalization of this argument. Consider any kite k = kite( f ) of the unfolding, and consider the path in the cut locus starting with vᵢ and ending with f. Apply the above proof to this path. The path will use one of the cut locus edges incident to vᵢ. The crucial observation is that wedge W in the statement of the lemma is a subset of wedge W₀ in the proof for this path. The proof shows that kite k does not enter wedge W₀, and therefore k does not enter W. □

  original_leaves : ∀ u : T.vertices, (u : Space) ∈ P.vertices → ∃! v, T.graph.Adj u v
  frames : CutTreeFrames T triangles
  covers : ∀ b : frontier P.body, ∃ u v : T.vertices, ∃ edge : T.graph.Adj u v,
    b ∈ (triangles edge).region
